Read About Lagos Nigeria

A fishing village on a lagoon that became Africa's largest city in under two centuries — and why Lagos continues to resist every attempt to define, tame, or slow it down.

A lagoon city the Portuguese named but did not build

Portuguese explorers reached the coast of what is now southwestern Nigeria in the 1470s, naming the large tidal lagoon they found Lago de Curamo — Lake of Curamo. The city that eventually took its name from that Portuguese rendering, Lagos, was already home before any European arrived. The Awori, a sub-group of the Yoruba people, had settled the island of Eko by the fourteenth century, living by fishing and trading along the lagoon's waterways. The Bini of the Kingdom of Benin, which controlled the area from the sixteenth century onward, called it Eko, a name still used by residents today.

Portuguese contact brought trade, but the nature of that trade shifted over the following centuries into something catastrophic. The lagoon's geography — deep enough for ocean-going vessels, screened from the open Atlantic by barrier islands, connected by waterways to the interior — made Lagos an almost ideal staging point for the Atlantic slave trade. The island of Badagry, west of Lagos proper, became one of the major ports through which enslaved Africans were transported. The Point of No Return at Badagry marks where the captives were loaded onto ships; the Seriki Abass Slave Barracoon nearby is where they were held. Estimates suggest that hundreds of thousands of people passed through this stretch of coastline during the trade's peak in the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries.

Cession, colonization, and the making of a capital

Britain officially abolished the slave trade in 1807 and began using naval patrols to suppress it. Lagos, however, remained an active trade point under the Oba Kosoko, who resisted British pressure to end the practice. In 1851, the British Navy bombarded the island and deposed Kosoko, installing the more cooperative Oba Akitoye. A decade later, in 1861, a formal treaty — under disputed circumstances, with the Oba Dosunmu reportedly signing under duress — ceded Lagos Island to the British Crown. It became the Colony of Lagos.

The colonial city grew rapidly, partly because of its function as the principal port for the entire region. The Lagos-Kano railway, begun in 1896 and extended in stages, tied the coast to the northern interior, making Lagos the natural export point for groundnuts, cotton, tin, and palm oil. Freed enslaved people and their descendants — the Saro, returning from Sierra Leone, and the Aguda, returning from Brazil — formed an educated, entrepreneurial class that built the distinctive Brazilian-influenced townhouses still visible on Lagos Island today. Carter Bridge, completed in 1901, was the first fixed link between Lagos Island and the mainland. By the time Nigeria became a republic in 1963, Lagos was already the country's commercial engine.

Independence, oil, and an unrepeatable decade

Nigeria became independent in 1960, with Lagos as its capital. The discovery of commercially viable oil deposits in the Niger Delta in the late 1950s transformed the national economy, and Lagos, as the commercial capital, absorbed much of the resulting wealth and migration. The population, roughly 300,000 in 1950, surpassed a million by the late 1960s. The Eko Bridge opened in 1975, and the Third Mainland Bridge — at the time one of the longest bridges in Africa — opened in 1990, connecting the island to the sprawling mainland settlements.

Nigeria's capital was moved to the planned city of Abuja in 1991, but the transfer barely slowed Lagos. Commerce, banking, media, and entertainment stayed where they were. The city continued to draw migrants from across Nigeria and West Africa at a pace that planners could not keep up with. Today, with a metropolitan population estimated between 15 and 25 million depending on how the urban boundary is drawn, Lagos is consistently ranked among the ten largest cities in the world — and the largest in Africa.

Afrobeats, Nollywood, and a creative explosion

Lagos has long been a cultural capital, but the past two decades have brought that reputation to a global audience. Nollywood — the Nigerian film industry centered in Lagos — produces more films annually than Hollywood and is second only to Bollywood in output. The films are shot cheaply and quickly, distributed first through street vendors on disc and now through streaming, and they reach audiences across sub-Saharan Africa, the Nigerian diaspora, and beyond. The industry is estimated to employ more than a million people in Nigeria.

Afrobeats, the genre that fuses Yoruba musical traditions with West African highlife, American hip-hop and R&B, and electronic production, was forged in Lagos clubs and studios. The New Afrika Shrine in Ikeja, which Fela Kuti's son Femi rebuilt after the original was destroyed by soldiers in 1977, remains the spiritual home of the genre. Artists like Burna Boy, Wizkid, Davido, and Tiwa Savage, all Lagos-rooted, have turned Afrobeats into a worldwide phenomenon over the past decade. The Shrine on a Thursday night, with musicians warming up before midnight and the main act going until four in the morning, is unlike any venue in the world.

Art, craft, and the island that never stops making things

The Nike Art Gallery on Lekki Peninsula is a direct expression of one woman's determination to preserve Yoruba visual traditions. Nike Davies-Okundaye began as a traditional tie-dye artist, eventually building a complex that now houses thousands of works of art across five floors — sculptures, textiles, photographs, paintings, and beadwork — while simultaneously training hundreds of young artists in traditional crafts. The gallery is not a museum in the Western sense; it is a living workshop, a commercial enterprise, a cultural institution, and a personal archive all at once.

Terra Kulture on Victoria Island takes a complementary approach: its restaurant, gallery, and performance space are built around Yoruba language instruction and the idea that language and art are inseparable. The National Museum Lagos in Onikan holds the Benin Bronzes that remain in Nigeria — a fraction of the collection taken by British troops in 1897, some of which are still held in Western institutions, a dispute that remains unresolved. Freedom Park on Lagos Island was the site of Broad Street Prison, a colonial-era jail; it is now a garden and performance venue, with the original prison walls still standing as ruins around the perimeter.

The geography that shapes everything

Lagos is not one place but an archipelago of islands, peninsulas, and mainland settlements connected by a network of bridges and roads that struggle to absorb the daily movement of millions of people. Traffic, known locally simply as go-slow, is a defining feature of daily life. The solution for some residents is the boat — the lagoon still functions as a transport corridor, with private water taxis and ferry services connecting points that would take an hour by road in minutes by water.

Victoria Island and Ikoyi, both connected to Lagos Island by bridge, house the city's financial institutions, embassies, and upscale residential neighborhoods. Lekki, further along the peninsula to the east, is newer money — gated estates, shopping malls, and the conservation centre where a canopy walkway above the forest offers a view of the city at its most improbable: dense green treetops with the Atlantic coast visible in one direction and the lagoon in the other. The mainland — Ikeja, Yaba, Surulere, Oshodi — is where most of the city actually lives and works, where the markets function at a scale that requires a full day to walk through, and where the energy that powers Lagos is generated.
